text: The LORD said to Moses:
Speak to the Israelites and say to them: When anyone makes a special vow to the LORD involving the value set on a person,
the value for a male between twenty and sixty years old shall be fifty shekels of silver, by the sanctuary shekel.
If it is a female, the value shall be thirty shekels.
For someone between five and twenty years old, the value for a male shall be twenty shekels and for a female ten shekels.
For a child between one month and five years old, the value for a male shall be five shekels of silver and for a female three shekels of silver.
For someone sixty years old or over, the value for a male shall be fifteen shekels and for a female ten shekels.
If the person is too poor to pay the set value, he shall be brought before the priest, and the priest shall set the value according to what the one making the vow can afford.

versions.text: If the one who made the vow is too poor to pay the set value, he shall present the person before the priest, and the priest shall set the value according to what the one making the vow can afford.
versions.explanation: In the Hebrew, the subject of 'too poor' is the one being valued (הוּא), who is then stood before the priest. The current wording makes the vower both the poor one and the presenter, which adds interpretation and creates an awkward doubling of 'the one who made the vow / the one making the vow' in one sentence.

text: If the vow concerns an animal that may be offered to the LORD, every such animal given to the LORD becomes holy.
He must not exchange it or substitute a good one for a bad one, or a bad one for a good one. If he does substitute one animal for another, both it and its substitute become holy.
If the vow concerns an unclean animal, one that may not be offered to the LORD, the animal shall be presented before the priest,
and the priest shall set its value, whether high or low. Whatever value the priest sets shall stand.
If the owner does redeem it, he must add a fifth to the set value.

versions.text: If the owner wishes to redeem it, he must add a fifth to its value.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew infinitive absolute construction expresses actual redemption ('if he indeed redeems it') rather than a wish; 'wishes to' is repeated in verses 15, 19, and 31 as well. Also 'the set value' better renders עֶרְכֶּךָ, the priest's assessed price.

text: If anyone dedicates his house as holy to the LORD, the priest shall set its value, whether high or low. Whatever the priest sets, that is what it shall be.
If the one who dedicated the house wishes to redeem it, he must add a fifth to its value in silver, and it shall be his again.
If anyone dedicates to the LORD part of the field he has inherited, its value shall be set according to the seed required for it: fifty shekels of silver for each homer of barley seed.
If he dedicates his field during the Year of Jubilee, the full value shall stand.
But if he dedicates it after the Jubilee, the priest shall calculate the price according to the years remaining until the next Year of Jubilee, and the value shall be reduced accordingly.
If the one who dedicated the field wishes to redeem it, he must add a fifth to its value in silver, and it shall revert to him.
But if he does not redeem the field, or if he has sold it to someone else, it can never be redeemed.
When the field is released in the Jubilee, it becomes holy to the LORD, like a field placed under the ban; it shall become the priest's holding.

versions.text: When the field is released in the Jubilee, it becomes holy to the LORD, like a field devoted to him; it shall become the property of the priests.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has the singular 'the priest' (לַכֹּהֵן), not 'the priests', and אֲחֻזָּתוֹ is the technical term 'holding/inherited property' used throughout the chapter. 'Field devoted to him' also weakens the technical sense of חֵרֶם (irrevocably devoted, placed under the ban).

text: If anyone dedicates to the LORD a field he has bought, one that is not part of his inherited land,
the priest shall calculate its value up to the Year of Jubilee, and the man shall pay that amount on that day as something holy to the LORD.
In the Year of Jubilee the field shall return to the one from whom it was bought, the one whose inherited land it is.
Every value shall be set by the sanctuary shekel: twenty gerahs to the shekel.
But no one may dedicate the firstborn of an animal, since as a firstborn it already belongs to the LORD; whether ox or sheep, it is the LORD's.

versions.text: But no one may dedicate the firstborn of an animal, since the firstborn already belongs to the LORD; whether ox or sheep, it is the LORD's.
versions.explanation: Minor clarity: the Hebrew stresses that the animal is the LORD's precisely by virtue of being firstborn. The current sentence repeats 'the firstborn' twice awkwardly for oral reading.

text: If it is an unclean animal, the owner may buy it back at its set value, adding a fifth to it; if it is not redeemed, it shall be sold at its set value.

versions.text: If it is an unclean animal, it may be bought back at its set value, with a fifth added; if it is not redeemed, it shall be sold at its set value.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb פָּדָה is active with the owner as subject; the active construction also reads more naturally aloud and avoids the vague dangling phrase 'with a fifth added'.

text: But nothing that a person devotes to the LORD from all he owns—whether human being or animal or inherited land—may be sold or redeemed. Everything so devoted is most holy to the LORD.
No person who has been devoted to destruction may be ransomed; he must be put to death.
Every tithe of the land, whether from the seed of the ground or the fruit of the trees, belongs to the LORD; it is holy to the LORD.
If anyone wishes to redeem part of his tithe, he must add a fifth to it.
Every tithe of the herd and flock—of all that passes under the shepherd's rod, every tenth animal—shall be holy to the LORD.

versions.text: Every tithe of the herd and flock—every tenth animal that passes under the shepherd's rod—shall be holy to the LORD.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew distinguishes two clauses: all the animals pass under the rod, and the tenth one is holy. The current rendering makes 'every tenth animal' the one passing under the rod, which reverses the sense.

text: He must not examine whether it is good or bad, nor make any substitution. If he does substitute one for another, both it and its substitute become holy and cannot be redeemed.

versions.text: He must not pick out the good from the bad or make any substitution. If he does substitute one for another, both it and its substitute become holy and cannot be redeemed.
versions.explanation: יְבַקֵּר means to inspect or examine; the point is that the owner must not sort the animals by quality to keep the better ones. 'Pick out the good from the bad' could be read as forbidding selection rather than inspection.

text: These are the commandments the LORD gave Moses on Mount Sinai for the Israelites.
